questions.q: What problem does calling vector.reserve(n) before a loop of push_back calls solve?
options: It sorts the vector's elements before inserting
It avoids the repeated reallocate-and-copy cycles that occur as push_back grows the vector past its current capacity
It makes the vector thread-safe
It converts the vector into a std::array
questions.explain: Without reserve, a vector growing via push_back periodically reallocates a larger buffer and copies every existing element into it. reserve(n) performs one allocation up front, eliminating those repeated reallocation-and-copy cycles.

questions.q: Why is `double sum(const std::vector<double>& prices)` generally preferable to `double sum(std::vector<double> prices)` when the function only reads the vector?
options: The const& version is required for the code to compile
The const& version avoids making a full copy of the vector just to call the function
The by-value version cannot iterate over the vector's elements
const& automatically parallelizes the loop inside the function
questions.explain: Passing by value for a large object like a std::vector copies all of its elements just to invoke the function. Passing by const reference gives read-only access to the original data with no copy at all.

questions.q: What does std::move(local) do to the variable `local`?
options: It deletes `local` from memory immediately
It casts `local` to an rvalue reference, signaling that its internal resources may be transferred rather than copied; `local` is left in a valid but unspecified state afterward
It makes a deep copy of `local` and returns the copy
It converts `local` into a const reference
questions.explain: std::move itself doesn't move anything — it's a cast that enables move construction/assignment to transfer the source object's internal resources instead of copying them. After the move, the source is left valid but typically empty or unspecified.

questions.q: According to the lesson's rule of thumb, which parameter-passing style should be used for a small, cheap-to-copy type like `int` or `double`?
options: Always pass by const&, even for built-in types
Pass by value — the copy cost is negligible for small types
Always pass by std::move
Pass by non-const reference by default
questions.explain: For small, cheap-to-copy types such as built-in numeric types, passing by value is simple and costs essentially nothing — the overhead of a reference provides no real benefit and can even be slightly worse.

questions.q: When a function returns a local std::vector by value in modern C++, what typically happens to the vector's data?
options: It is always deep-copied into the caller's variable
It is moved (or elided entirely) into the caller's variable, avoiding a copy
It is leaked, since local variables cannot be returned
It is serialized to disk and reloaded by the caller
questions.explain: Modern C++ compilers apply move semantics (and often copy elision) when returning a local object by value, transferring ownership of the underlying buffer to the caller's variable instead of performing an expensive deep copy.
